messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 68
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Non-profit Worker
- Trauma Type: Rape
- Pcl5: 76

He is a 68-year-old South Asian man who speaks about his life in a careful, measured way, as though each word has to be checked before it is allowed out. He works in a non-profit role that he has held for many years, helping recent immigrants navigate housing, benefits, and paperwork. His work has always been a source of purpose for him, a way to remain useful after his divorce and long after his children grew up. He describes himself as someone who has always tried to be steady for others, even when his own life felt unsettled.

The assault happened in adulthood, after a period in which he had already been feeling isolated and ashamed about the collapse of his marriage. He had gone to see someone he knew from the community, believing he was entering a private and ordinary conversation. Instead, he was raped. He speaks of the event with a flatness that makes the horror more apparent, as if the facts are kept at a distance because they are too unbearable to inhabit directly. In the days afterward, he did not tell anyone. He showered repeatedly, scrubbed his skin, and changed his clothes more than once a day, but the feeling of being contaminated did not lift. He began sleeping lightly, waking at every sound, and he found himself sitting in the dark for long stretches because going to bed meant having to face what his mind would bring back.

At work, he tried to continue as if nothing had happened. He kept appointments, answered calls, and helped clients fill out forms, but he noticed that he could not concentrate the way he used to. He would read the same line several times without taking it in. A knock on the office door could make his chest seize. If someone stood behind him too quietly, he would tense before he knew why. He started positioning himself closer to exits and checking locks more than once. He says he became “a careful man,” but the care had the quality of vigilance, not calm.

Over time, the memories began to arrive without warning. A smell in a hallway, a phrase spoken in a certain tone, the sense of being alone with a man who seemed friendly—each could pull him back into the assault with such force that he would freeze or lose track of where he was. He describes moments when the office, the street, or his own bedroom would suddenly feel unreal, as though he were standing outside his body watching himself move through a life that no longer belonged to him. He hates these episodes most when they happen in public, because he can feel himself becoming distant and then have to reconstruct what just occurred.

He has also become more irritable and more withdrawn. Friends invite him to gatherings, and he often declines, saying he is tired or busy. In truth, crowds make him feel trapped. He used to enjoy walking to the market and talking with familiar shopkeepers; now he chooses the quietest times and leaves quickly. He no longer trusts ease. He wonders if others can see something in him that he cannot hide. Shame remains central in the way he speaks about the assault, especially because of his cultural expectations about masculinity, privacy, and family honor. He says that for a long time he felt less like a victim than a failure, and this belief made it difficult to confide in anyone, including his adult children.

At night, he often lies awake replaying the event and imagining what he should have done differently. His thoughts turn harsh and repetitive. He blames himself for going there, for not recognizing danger sooner, for not fighting harder, for surviving. Some nights he drinks tea until dawn and sits in the kitchen because sleep feels like surrender. He has become startle-prone and exhausted, and the fatigue has made him slower at work, which in turn deepens his worry that he is no longer the dependable man his clients and colleagues have come to expect.

Despite everything, he continues to show up. He arrives at the non-profit office before others, organizes files, and greets people gently. He knows the routines of helping better than he knows how to rest. He says that work gives him a structure sturdy enough to hold him together for a few hours at a time. Yet even there, he remains alert to danger, scanning faces, listening for tone, measuring distance. He lives in the aftermath of the assault as though safety is something provisional, always about to be withdrawn, and each day requires him to negotiate between his desire to disappear and his stubborn decision to remain.
